In [[differential topology]] in mathematics, '''Donaldson invariants''' are [[Invariant (mathematics)|invariants]] of the smooth structure of four-[[Dimension|dimensional]] [[smooth manifolds]] (short [[4-manifold|4-manifolds]]) based on the methods behind [[Donaldson's theorem]]. In particular, key informations are obtained from the [[Yang–Mills moduli space]] of the [[Yang–Mills equations]] on the 4-manifold, which as [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]] depend on the smooth structure. Donaldson invariants can distinguish these, hence are able to detect exotic smooth structures, meaning explicitly that [[Homeomorphism|homeomorphic]] smooth 4-manifolds, hence identical from a topological perspective, can nonetheless have different Donaldson invariants. Donaldson invariants are named after [[Simon Donaldson]], who first described Donaldson's theorem in 1983<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Donaldson|first=Simon|author-link=Simon Donaldson|date=1983|title=An application of gauge theory to four-dimensional topology|journal=[[Journal of Differential Geometry]]|volume=18|issue=2|doi=10.4310/jdg/1214437665|issn=0022-040X}}</ref> (with improvement in 1987<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Donaldson|first=Simon|author-link=Simon Donaldson|date=1987|title=The orientation of Yang-Mills moduli spaces and 4-manifold topology|journal=[[Journal of Differential Geometry]]|volume=26|issue=3|doi=10.4310/jdg/1214441485|issn=0022-040X|s2cid=120208733}}</ref>) and the resulting invariants in 1986. He was also awarded a [[Fields Medal]] for his contributions in 1986.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Fields Medals 1986 - Donaldson, Faltings, Freedman Achievements |url=https://www.mathunion.org/imu-awards/fields-medal/fields-medals-1986 |access-date=2026-07-04 |website=www.mathunion.org}}</ref>

== History ==

[[File:Simon Donaldson.jpg|thumb|Simon Donaldson was awarded the [[Fields Medal]] in 1986<ref name=":3" /> for the development of Donaldson theory]]
[[File:Witten at Chalmers2.jpg|thumb|Edward Witten was awarded the Fields Medal in 1990<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fields Medals 1990 - Breakthroughs in Mathematics and Physics |url=https://www.mathunion.org/imu-awards/fields-medal/fields-medals-1990 |access-date=2026-07-04 |website=www.mathunion.org}}</ref> for the development of topological quantum field theories (TQFT)<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last=Witten|first=Edward|title=Topological quantum field theory|journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics|volume=117|issue=3|pages=353–386|bibcode=1988CMaPh.117..353W|doi=10.1007/BF01223371|mr=0953828|s2cid=43230714}}</ref>]]

In 1983<ref name=":4" /> (with later improvement in 1987<ref name=":5" />), [[Simon Donaldson]] proved [[Donaldson's theorem]] with the unexpected strategy of using the (anti) self-dual [[Yang–Mills moduli space]] ((A)SDYM moduli space) of [[Principal SU(2)-bundle|principal SU(2)-bundles]], hence with the [[special unitary group]] <math>\operatorname{SU}(2)</math> as [[structure group]]. In 1984, [[Ronald Fintushel]] und [[Ronald Stern]] adapted his work to [[Principal SO(3)-bundle|principal SO(3)-bundles]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fintushel |first=Ronald |author-link=Ronald Fintushel |last2=Stern |first2=Ronald |author-link2=Ronald J. Stern |date=1984 |title=SO(3)-connections and the topology of 4-manifolds |url=https://bpb-us-e2.wpmucdn.com/faculty.sites.uci.edu/dist/3/246/files/2011/03/21_So3_connections.pdf |journal=[[Journal of Differential Geometry]] |volume=20 |pages=523–539}}</ref> hence with the special orthogonal group <math>\operatorname{SO}(3)</math> as structure group. Both groups are connected by a double cover <math>\operatorname{SU}(2)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{SO}(3)</math>, exactly the [[adjoint representation]], alternatively phrased one has the third [[spin group]] <math>\operatorname{Spin}(3)\cong\operatorname{SU}(2)</math> and the second [[projective unitary group]] <math>\operatorname{PU}(2)\cong\operatorname{SO}(3)</math>. In 1986, Simon Donaldson expanded his work into [[Invariant (mathematics)|invariants]] about the smooth structure of smooth manifolds, which work with both structure groups <math>\operatorname{SU}(2)</math> and <math>\operatorname{SO}(3)</math>. In 1988, [[Edward Witten]] opened up the field of [[Topological quantum field theory|topological quantum field theories]] (TQFT)<ref name=":8" /> and showed, that Donaldson invariants can be expressed as the [[Expectation value (quantum mechanics)|expectation values]] of a topologically twisted [[N = 2 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory]] (TT D = 4 N = 2 SYM).

In early 1994, [[Peter Kronheimer]] and [[Tomasz Mrowka]] achieved a strong simplification of Donaldson invariants with the introduction of [[Kronheimer–Mrowka basic class|Kronheimer–Mrowka basic classes]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kronheimer |first=Peter |author-link=Peter B. Kronheimer |last2=Mrowka |first2=Tomasz |author-link2=Tomasz Mrowka |date=1994 |title=Recurrence relations and asymptotics for four-manifold invariants |journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=30 |issue=2 |pages=215–221 |arxiv=math/9404232 |doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-1994-00492-6}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kronheimer |first=Peter |author-link=Peter B. Kronheimer |last2=Mrowka |first2=Tomasz |author-link2=Tomasz Mrowka |date=1995 |title=Embedded surfaces and the structure of Donaldson's polynomial invariants |journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=41 |issue=3 |pages=573–734 |doi=10.4310/jdg/1214456482}}</ref> which reduced its [[Infinite sum|infinite sums]] to finite sums. In late 1994, [[Nathan Seiberg]] and Edward Witten constructed the dual TT N = 2 SYM.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Seiberg |first=Nathan |author-link=Nathan Seiberg |last2=Witten |first2=Edward |author-link2=Edward Witten |title=Electric-Magnetic Duality, Monopole Condensation, and Confinement in N = 2 Supersymmetric Yang-Mills Theory |journal=[[Nuclear Physics B]] |volume=426 |issue=1 |pages=19–52 |arxiv=hep-th/9407087 |doi=10.1016/0550-3213%2894%2990124-4}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Seiberg |first=Nathan |author-link=Nathan Seiberg |last2=Witten |first2=Edward |author-link2=Edward Witten |date=1994 |title=Monopoles, Duality and Chiral Symmetry Breaking in N = 2 Supersymmetric QCD |journal=[[Nuclear Physics B]] |volume=431 |pages=484–550 |arxiv=hep-th/9408099 |doi=10.1016/0550-3213%2894%2990214-3}}</ref><ref>Scorpan 05, p. 356</ref><ref>Naber 2011, p. 362-363</ref> Both this gauge theory as well as its application to four-dimensional geometry are often referred to as [[Seiberg–Witten theory]], but strictly speaking are two different theories. [[Seiberg–Witten invariants]] brought multiple improvements over Donaldson invariants, mainly due to the easier and furthermore [[Abelian group|abelian]] [[unitary group]] <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math> as structure group or the always [[Compact space|compact]] [[Seiberg–Witten moduli space]], with made laborious [[Compactification (mathematics)|compactifications]] using [[Uhlenbeck's compactness theorem]] required for Donaldson invariants obsolete. Despite that, it could be shown in the following years that Seiberg–Witten invariants still contain more information than Donaldson invariants, so the latter are not used as actively any more. In particular, [[Clifford Taubes]] described a connection to [[Gromov–Witten invariant|Gromov–Witten invariants]] and Edward Witten concluded from purely physical arguments the Witten conjecture, that Kronheimer–Mrowka basic classes and therefore Donaldson invariants can be fully obtained from Seiberg–Witten theory.<ref>Naber 2011, p. 398-400</ref>

By now, also topologically twisted four-dimensional [[N = 4 supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory|N = 4 supersymmetric Yang–Mills theories]] (TT D = 4 N = 4 SYM) are considered, including [[Donaldson–Witten theory]], [[Vafa–Witten theory]] and [[Kapustin–Witten theory]], with other variants like three-dimensional [[Rozansky–Witten theory]]. From these, further invariants like [[Vafa–Witten invariants]] and [[Rozansky–Witten invariants]] arise, with current research trying to determine how they expand and improve the original idea of Donaldson invariants.

== SU(2) Donaldson invariants ==
Let <math>X</math> be an [[Orientability|oriented]] [[Closed manifold|closed]] [[Smooth manifold|smooth]] [[4-manifold]] and <math>P\twoheadrightarrow X</math> be a [[principal SU(2)-bundle]], then there exists a unique [[homotopy class]] represented by a classifying map <math>\tau\colon X\rightarrow\operatorname{BSU}(2)\cong\mathbb{H}P^\infty</math> into the [[Classifying space for SU(n)|classifying space for SU(2)]] giving a pullback <math>P=\tau^*\operatorname{ESU}(2)=\tau^*S^\infty</math>. With the [[Kronecker pairing]] and the [[fundamental class]] <math>[X]\in H_4(X,\mathbb{Z})</math> from the orientation, the second [[Chern class]] concretely gives a [[group isomorphism]]:

: <math>
\langle c_2(-),[X]\rangle\colon
\operatorname{Prin}_{\operatorname{SU}(2)}(X)\xrightarrow\cong\mathbb{Z}.
</math>

Let <math>\mathcal{A}:=\Omega_{\operatorname{Ad}}^1(P,\mathfrak{su}(2))</math> be the configuration space of connections on <math>P</math>, which is an [[Affine space|affine vector space]] not canonically isomorphic to <math>\Omega^1(X,\operatorname{Ad}(P))</math>. Let <math>\mathcal{G}:=\operatorname{Aut}_{\operatorname{SU}(2)}(P)</math> be the [[Gauge group (mathematics)|gauge group]] of [[gauge transformations]] of <math>P</math>, which acts on <math>\mathcal{A}</math>. Let <math>\mathcal{B}:=\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{G}</math> be the [[orbit space]],<ref>Donaldson 86, Eq. (2.1)</ref><ref name=":0">Naber 2011, p. 352-355</ref> then there is a [[weak homotopy equivalence]] <math>\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\operatorname{Map}_P(X,\operatorname{BSU}(2))</math> in the homotopy class of the classifying map of <math>P</math>.<ref>Donaldson 86, Lem. (2.4)</ref><ref>Donaldson & Kronheimer 97, Prop. 5.1.4</ref> [[Currying]] it corresponds to a map <math>\mathcal{B}\times X\rightarrow\operatorname{BSU}(2)</math> and through pullback a principal <math>\operatorname{SU}(2)</math>-bundle <math>\widetilde{P}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{B}\times X</math>.<ref>Donaldson & Kronheimer 97, Eq. (5.1.5)</ref> For every gauge class <math>[A]\in\mathcal{B}</math>, one has <math>\widetilde{P}\vert_{\{[A]\}\times X}\cong P\twoheadrightarrow X</math>. With the second Chern class <math>c_2(\widetilde{P})\in H^4(\mathcal{B}\times X,\mathbb{Z})</math>, the [[slant product]] yields a map:<ref>Donaldson 86, Def. 2.5</ref><ref>Freed & Uhlenbeck 91, p. xi-xii</ref><ref name=":7">Donaldson & Kronheimer 97, p. 176-177</ref><ref name=":0" />
: <math>
\mu\colon
H_2(X,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^2(\mathcal{B},\mathbb{Z}),
\mu(\alpha):=c_2(\widetilde{P})/\alpha.
</math>
[[File:Donaldson's Theorem cobordism.png|thumb|Visualization<ref name=":6">Freed & Uhlenbeck 1984, p. 45-46</ref><ref>Donaldson & Kronheimer 1990, p. 326</ref> of the five-dimensional self-dual Yang–Mills moduli space from the proof of Donaldson's theorem]]
With the subset <math>\mathcal{M}\subset\mathcal{B}</math> of an (anti) self-dual [[Yang–Mills moduli space]] there is an induced map <math>H^2(\mathcal{B},\mathbb{Z})\hookrightarrow H^2(\mathcal{M},\mathbb{Z})</math>, which through postcomposition yields a map <math>\mu\colon H_2(X,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^2(\mathcal{M},\mathbb{Z})</math>. With the interpretation of the homology classes as embedded surfaces <math>i\colon\Sigma\hookrightarrow M</math> with <math>i_*[\Sigma]\in H_2(M,\mathbb{Z})</math> and the interpretation of the cohomology classes as [[Differential form|differential forms]] of second order using [[de Rham cohomology]] <math>H^2(\mathcal{M},\mathbb{R})\cong H_\mathrm{dR}^2(\mathcal{M})</math>, one can see the map <math>\mu</math> as mapping embedded surfaces in <math>M</math> to differential forms of second order in <math>\mathcal{M}</math>. Donaldson invariants are defined using the integration of these differential forms, which is disrupted by the missing compatness and the singularities of the moduli space. A compactification <math>\mathcal{M}\subset\overline\mathcal{M}</math> can be constructed using [[Uhlenbeck's compactness theorem]] and leads to a <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-linear map <math>\mu\colon H_2(X,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^2(\overline\mathcal{M},\mathbb{Z})</math>.<ref name=":02">Naber 2011, p. 352-355</ref>

Let <math>P_k\twoheadrightarrow X</math> be the unique principal <math>\operatorname{SU}(2)</math>-bundle with <math>\langle c_2(P_k),[X]\rangle=k</math> according to the above group isomorphism, then <math>\langle p_1\operatorname{Ad}(P_k),[X]\rangle=-4k</math> for the first Pontrjagin class of the [[Adjoint bundle|adjoint vector bundle]] and the virtual dimension of its anti self-dual Yang–Mills (ASDYM) moduli space is given with the [[Atiyah–Singer index theorem]] by:<ref name=":2">Salamon 99, p. 262-265</ref><ref name=":1">Scorpan 05, p. 355</ref><ref name=":03">Naber 2011, p. 352-355</ref>

: <math>
\dim\mathcal{M}_k
=-8k-3(1-b_1(M)+b_2^+(M)).
</math>

If <math>-b_1(M)+b_2^+(M)</math> is odd, then the virtual dimension is an even number <math>\dim\mathcal{M}_k
=2d_k</math>,<ref name=":03" /> potentially negative given the choice of <math>k</math>. With a fundamental class <math>\left[\mathcal{M}_k\right]\in H_{2d_k}(\mathcal{M}_k,\mathbb{Z})
\cong\mathbb{Z}^{b_0\left(\mathcal{M}_k\right)}</math> since the ASDYM moduli space is orientable, the Donaldson invariant is given with the [[cup product]] and the Kronecker pairing:<ref name=":03" /><ref name=":1" />

: <math>
\mathcal{D}_{X,k}\colon
\operatorname{Sym}^{d_k}H_2(X,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow\mathbb{Z},
\mathcal{D}_{X,k}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_{d_k}):=\left\langle\mu(\alpha_1)\smile\ldots\smile\mu(\alpha_{d_k}), \left[\mathcal{M}_k\right]\right\rangle.</math>

Considering the second homology classes in a symmetric setting only up to [[permutation]] comes from the symmetry of the cup product, hence the irrelevance of any order. It can furthermore be shown, that the Donaldson invariants also don't depend on the [[Riemannian metric]] and therefore only on the smooth structure.

== Change of instanton number ==
According to the above formula, <math>\dim\mathcal{M}_{k+1}=\dim\mathcal{M}_k+8</math> holds under a change of the instanton number, expanding the input of the Donaldson invariant by four new second homology classes. More generally, the slant product yields a <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-linear map <math>\mu\colon H_n(X,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^{4-n}(\overline\mathcal{M},\mathbb{Z})</math>,<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":22">Salamon 99, p. 262-265</ref><ref name=":12">Scorpan 05, p. 355</ref> so for <math>X</math> connected with <math>H_0(X,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}</math> a map <math>\mu\colon\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow H^4(\overline\mathcal{M},\mathbb{Z})</math>. Hence one can also expand the Donaldson invariant by two images of a generator.

== SO(3) Donaldson invariants ==
Let <math>P\twoheadrightarrow X</math> be a [[principal SO(3)-bundle]], then there exists a unique homotopy class represented by a classifying map <math>\tau\colon X\rightarrow\operatorname{BSO}(3)</math> into the [[Classifying space for SO(n)|classifying space for SO(3)]] giving a pullback <math>P=\tau^*\operatorname{ESO}(3)</math>. Now the second [[Stiefel–Whitney class]] and the first [[Pontryagin class|Pontrjagin class]] give a group isomorphism:

: <math>
(w_2,\langle p_1(-),[X]\rangle)\colon
\operatorname{Prin}_{\operatorname{SO}(3)}(X)\xrightarrow\cong\{(v,n)\in H^2(X,\mathbb{Z}_2)\times\mathbb{Z}|\langle v^2,[X]\rangle\equiv n\operatorname{mod}4\}.
</math>

In this case, the first Pontrjagin class replaces the second Chern class in the slant product.

== Donaldson invariants of compactification ==

=== Compactification to two dimensions ===

According to the classification of surfaces, every oriented closed 2-manifold (surface) is homeomorphic to a Sigma surface <math>\Sigma_g=\# gT^2</math>, given as a connected sum of 2-tori <math>T^2=S^1\times S^1</math> with the convention <math>\Sigma_0=S^2</math>. Now the Donaldson invariants can be considered on the 4-manifold <math>\Sigma_g\times S^2</math>.

=== Compactification to three dimensions ===

For an oriented closed 3-manifold <math>Y</math>, one can consider the Donaldson invariants on the 4-manifold <math>Y\times S^1</math>. For general structure groups, they relate to the [[Rozansky–Witten invariant]]s of <math>Y</math> and for the structure group <math>\operatorname{SU}(2)</math>, they relate to the [[Casson–Walker–Lescop invariant]] of <math>Y</math>.
